abstract.title: Summary
abstract.p: The prognosis for patients with relapsed/refractory (R/R) adult T‐cell leukaemia‐lymphoma (ATL) remains dismal. Recently, valemetostat, a dual inhibitor for enhancer of zeste homologue (EZH) 1 and 2, was approved in Japan for R/R aggressive ATL. However, there is no real‐world data on the efficacy and prognosis of valemetostat. We therefore analysed clinical outcomes in 28 patients with R/R aggressive ATL who received valemetostat at three hospitals in Kumamoto Prefecture between February 2023 and January 2025. The overall response rate (ORR) and complete response (CR) rate were 54.2% and 33.3% respectively. With a median follow‐up of 19.2 months (7.3–21.7) for surviving patients, the median survival time was 15.8 months and median progression‐free survival (PFS) was 8.3 months. The probabilities of 1‐year overall survival (OS) and PFS were 55.8% and 44.1% respectively. Furthermore, the probabilities of 1‐year duration of response and duration of CR were 56.2% and 71.4% respectively. Notably, the probability of 1‐year OS was 90.9% in patients who achieved CR/partial response (PR) (‘responders’) compared to 17.0% in patients who did not achieve CR/PR (p < 0.001). Thus, valemetostat has the potential to be a reliable therapy for patients with R/R aggressive ATL, especially for responders.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Adult T‐cell leukaemia‐lymphoma (ATL) is a malignant T‐cell leukaemia‐lymphoma with a poor prognosis, 1 , 2 , 3 caused by human T‐cell leukaemia virus type I. 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 Despite the recent advances in treatment strategies, 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 including intensive chemotherapy, 14 antiviral therapy, 15 , 16 allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo‐HSCT) 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 and molecular targeted agent combined with chemotherapies, 21 , 22 , 23 a high rate of relapsed/refractory (R/R) disease remains a prevalent challenge. 24 , 25 It is imperative to note that once the disease progresses to R/R, the prognosis is dismal, 26 , 27 , 28 , 29 underscoring the need for reliable treatment options for R/R ATL.

Monotherapy with mogamulizumab (Moga), an anti‐CC‐chemokine receptor 4 antibody, has improved survival to some extent for relapsed patients with ATL in Japan. 30 , 31 , 32 , 33 , 34 , 35 , 36 However, it remains largely unsatisfactory, especially in patients with a history of numerous prior treatment regimens or in those with refractory disease 31 , 37 : In particular, the median progression‐free survival (PFS) in the Moga monotherapy group was only 0.9 months in a multinational randomized controlled trial. 37 In addition, lenalidomide and tucidinostat have been utilized as therapeutic options for R/R ATL in Japan; however, their efficacy is limited, with median PFS of 3.8 and 1.9 months respectively. 38 , 39 Importantly, none of these three agents is approved for the treatment of ATL outside of Japan. Thus, there are limited options with durable responses for R/R ATL, resulting in the prognosis remaining poor.

In September 2022, valemetostat was approved in Japan for R/R aggressive ATL with an overall response rate (ORR) of 48% in a single‐arm phase II study. 40 Furthermore, valemetostat received approval in Japan in June 2024 for R/R peripheral T‐cell lymphoma (PTCL). 41 , 42 However, the treatment efficacy and prognostic impact of valemetostat in real‐world settings have remained unclear, since there are no reports from clinical practice.

In this study, we conducted a multicentre retrospective analysis to evaluate the therapeutic efficacy and clinical outcomes of patients with R/R aggressive ATL who received valemetostat. We highlight the beneficial impact of valemetostat on survival in patients with R/R ATL, especially in responders.

sec.title: Study design
sec.p: The present study was a multicentre, retrospective analysis of R/R patients with aggressive ATL who were treated with valemetostat between February 2023 and January 2025 at either Kumamoto University Hospital, National Hospital Organization Kumamoto Medical Center or Kumamoto Shinto General Hospital. We reviewed R/R patients with ATL during the study period and included all patients who received valemetostat treatment. Using this cohort of patients, we evaluated prognostic factors and treatment outcomes. The clinical data for each patient were extracted from the corresponding medical records. The soluble interleukin‐2 receptor (sIL‐2R) was generally examined monthly after valemetostat treatment.

The primary end‐points were overall survival (OS) and PFS. Secondary end‐points were time‐to‐next treatment (TTNT), best response to valemetostat and the duration of response (DOR)/duration of complete response (DOCR).

This study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Kumamoto University Hospital (No. 2226) and was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. The institutional review board at each participating institution provided its approval for this study.

sec.title: Definitions
sec.p: Clinical subtypes of ATL were classified according to the Shimoyama classification. 43 Patients with chronic‐type ATL and at least one clinical factor such as low serum albumin, high blood urea nitrogen or high serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) were classified as having unfavourable chronic‐type ATL. 43 Aggressive ATL included acute‐type, lymphoma‐type and unfavourable chronic‐type.

Response to treatment was defined in accordance with the criteria of the International Consensus Meeting. 44 Complete response (CR) was defined as resolution of all clinical, microscopic and radiographic evidence of ATL. Partial response (PR) was defined as a ≥50% reduction in the sum of the products of the largest diameters of measurable lesions and a ≥50% reduction in the number of abnormal lymphocytes in peripheral blood (PB), without the appearance of new lesions. Progressive disease (PD) was defined as a ≥50% increase in flower cells from the lowest number recorded, and an absolute lymphocyte count of ≥4 × 109/L and a ≥50% increase from nadir in the sum of the products of measurable disease. Stable disease (SD) was defined as all cases that did not meet the criteria for CR, PR or PD. Extranodal lesions were defined as non‐nodal lesions, excluding the skin and PB.

Disease status was defined by the same criteria as in the previous phase II study. 40 We re‐evaluated the response to treatment in all patients immediately prior to valemetostat, based on the criteria of the International Consensus. 44 Relapse, recurrent and refractory disease is defined as follows: disease progression after CR, PR and SD/PD, respectively, in response to treatment immediately prior to valemetostat.

sec.title: Treatment
sec.p: This study did not specifically define treatment strategies for ATL, although compliance with the current Japanese guidelines 45 and the International Consensus Meeting 9 , 44 was encouraged. Dose modifications of valemetostat were implemented by physicians according to the official prescribing information and appropriate use guidelines for valemetostat.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Categorical variables were compared using Fisher's exact test. Continuous variables were compared using the Mann–Whitney U‐test. The median follow‐up period was calculated using the reverse Kaplan–Meier method. The probability of survival outcomes was calculated using the Kaplan–Meier method, and the groups were compared using the log‐rank test. OS and PFS were defined as the time from the initiation of valemetostat administration to death from any cause or the date of last follow‐up, and to disease progression, or death from any cause respectively. TTNT was measured as the time from the initiation of valemetostat administration to subsequent change to a different treatment, death from any cause or last follow‐up. For responders, DOR/DOCR was calculated by the time from the date of first ORR/CR to the date of disease progression or last follow‐up. Adverse events (AEs) of the highest toxicity grade that occurred under valemetostat treatment were evaluated according to severity by the National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events, version 5.0. 46 We used the Cox proportional hazards model to evaluate risk factors for OS and PFS. Statistical significance was defined as a two‐sided p‐value of <0.05. Statistical analyses were performed using the EZR (v. 1.68; Saitama Medical Center, Jichi Medical University, Saitama, Japan), which is a graphical user interface for R (v.4.5.0; The R Foundation for Statistical Computing). 47

sec.title: Patient characteristics
sec.p: Patient inclusion flowchart is shown in Figure S1. During the study period, 28 patients with R/R aggressive ATL were treated with valemetostat. Clinical characteristics of these patients at diagnosis and at the time of valemetostat treatment are listed in Table S1 and Table 1 respectively. According to the Shimoyama classification, 43 15, 7 and 6 patients were identified as having the acute‐type, lymphoma‐type and unfavourable chronic‐type respectively. At diagnosis, 75% of the patients were classified as the intermediate/high risk according to the Adult T‐cell leukaemia‐lymphoma Prognostic Index (ATL‐PI), 48 while 50% were classified as high risk according to the Japan Clinical Oncology Group Prognostic Index. 49 At the time of valemetostat treatment, their median age was 74 years (range, 38–89 years), and 78.6% of patients were older than 70 years. Furthermore, 17.9% of patients exhibited poor performance status (PS) (2–4). The median time since the last treatment prior to valemetostat was 35.5 days (range, 10–1148), including 39.3% of patients who were refractory to their last treatment. In addition, the median number of regimens prior to valemetostat was three (range, 1–8), of which five patients (17.9%) and 19 patients (67.9%) had received allo‐HSCT and Moga respectively. One patient intended to proceed with allo‐HSCT and received it after valemetostat.

sec.title: Duration of valemetostat treatment
sec.p: The clinical courses and outcomes for each patient are shown in Figure 1. At the data cut‐off, the median duration of valemetostat administration was 6.0 months (range, 0.27–27.3 months). Of note, 11 patients have continued to receive valemetostat, including five patients for more than 20 months (ID: 1–5). Among the 17 patients who discontinued the drug, 13 had PD (ID: 6–8, 10, 11, 14–16, 19, 24, 25, 27, 28), two had AE (ID: 9, 12) and two were switched to best supportive care (BSC) owing to patient decision (ID: 13, 26). Five patients were treated for 28 days or less (two with PD [ID: 27, 28], two with switch to BSC [ID: 13, 26] and one with AE and then BSC [ID: 9]). A total of 17 patients underwent a reduction in dosage; however, 11 of these patients received valemetostat for more than 6.0 months.

sec.p: Response to valemetostat was evaluated in a total of 24 patients; four others were excluded: two patients who lacked computed tomography evaluation after valemetostat (ID: 13, 15), and two patients who achieved CR with prior treatment yet were treated with valemetostat because of increased sIL‐2R value (ID: 23) or increased ATL cells in PB with a lymphocyte count of less than 4 × 109/L (ID: 22) (Figure S1). The ORR and CR rate were 54.2% and 33.3% respectively (Table 2). The disease control rate (CR, PR and SD) was 83.3%. Notably, in patients with refractory disease after prior treatment, the ORR and CR rate were 45.5% and 36.4% respectively. Responses were consistent across disease sites: The ORR and CR rate were 50.0% and 25.0% for PB, 61.1% and 38.9% for nodal and/or extranodal lesions and 62.5% and 25.0% for skin lesions. In patients who achieved either CR or PR, the duration of valemetostat treatment was 8.4 months (range, 0.7–27.3), while for patients who achieved CR, it was 18.3 months (range, 0.7–27.3). In comparison, for patients who did not achieve either CR or PR, the duration of valemetostat treatment was only 2.1 months (range, 0.27–9.0) (Figure 1). All five patients who received valemetostat for 20 months or longer were responders.

sec.title: Survival outcomes
sec.p: The median follow‐up period of surviving patients was 19.2 months (range, 7.3–21.7 months). The probability of 1‐year OS and median survival time (MST) was 55.8% (95% confidence interval [CI], 32.8–73.7) and 15.8 months (95% CI, 9.8–not reached [NR]) respectively (Figure 2A). The probability of 1‐year PFS and median PFS was 44.1% (95% CI, 22.8–63.5) and 8.3 months (95% CI, 5.7–NR) (Figure 2B). The median TTNT was found to be 9.2 months (95% CI, 6.4–NR) (Figure 2C). Furthermore, in the responders, the probabilities of 1‐year DOR and DOCR were 56.2% (95% CI, 24.4–79.1) and 71.4% (95% CI, 25.8–92.0) respectively (Figure 2D,E).

sec.title: Prognostic factors
sec.p: Since the association between response to valemetostat and treatment duration (Figures 1 and 2D,E) was observed, a prognostic evaluation was conducted to further elucidate the matter. The probabilities of 1‐year OS and PFS were 90.9% (95% CI, 50.8–98.7) and 56.2% (95% CI, 24.4–79.1), respectively, in patients with CR/PR compared to 17.0% (95% CI, 0.9–51.0) and not available (NA) in patients with SD/PD (p < 0.001: Figure 3A and p = 0.01: Figure 3B). MST, median PFS and median TTNT were increasingly long for PD, SD, PR and CR, in that order, suggesting a close association between treatment efficacy and prognosis (p < 0.001, Figure S2A–C).

sec.p: Since sIL‐2R value is included in the ATL‐PI 48 and the modified ATL‐PI 50 and is potentially useful as tumour marker for ATL, 44 we evaluated the relationship of the reduction of sIL‐2R value after valemetostat treatment with survival outcomes. Among 26 patients with sIL‐2R levels above the upper limit of normal (ULN) at the initiation of valemetostat (two patients with sIL‐2R levels under the ULN were excluded, ID: 7,22; Figure S1), a reduction in sIL‐2R levels below the ULN was observed in 17 patients, with a median time of 1.3 months (range, 0.7–3.7 months) (Figure 1). Similar to treatment response, having an sIL‐2R level under the ULN following valemetostat treatment was associated with a better outcome. The probabilities of 1‐year OS and PFS in the sIL‐2R under ULN group were 72.7% (95% CI, 37.1–90.3) and 66.2% (95% CI, 32.4–86.0), respectively, while in the high sIL‐2R (>ULN) group, the corresponding probabilities were only 25.5% (95% CI, 4.1–55.7) and NA (95% CI, NA–NA) (p < 0.001 and p < 0.001; Figure 3C,D).

Regarding clinical factors prior to the administration of valemetostat, no statistically significant prognostic disparities were observed based on older age, the Shimoyama classification, disease status, the number of prior treatment lines, the presence/absence of prior Moga treatment, LDH value, sIL‐2R value or the presence/absence of dose reduction (Table S2). Only response to valemetostat and the reduction in sIL‐2R values after valemetostat were identified as significant prognostic factors for survival outcomes (Table S2).

sec.title: Adverse events
sec.p: Treatment‐emergent AEs observed in 28 patients are listed in Table S3. The most common AEs of all grades were dysgeusia (50%), alopecia (14.3%), infection (14.3%), neutropenia (17.9%), leucopenia (14.3%), thrombocytopenia (57.1%) and anaemia (28.6%). Of these, grade ≥ III AEs were infections (10.7%), thrombocytopenia (25.0%) and anaemia (10.7%). The most frequent AEs leading to interruption of valemetostat were infection (10.7%) and thrombocytopenia (10.7%), and those leading to reduction were thrombocytopenia (17.9%). Two patients discontinued due to AEs (one, diarrhoea; another, thrombocytopenia). No treatment‐related deaths were observed. Among the five transplanted patients, one patient exhibited grade II graft‐versus‐host disease in the skin. The duration from allo‐HSCT to valemetostat treatment in this patient was 1.3 months, whereas in the other four patients, it was over 6 months (6.9, 11.2, 12.0 and 52.0 months).

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: Here, we demonstrate that valemetostat offers a new paradigm for the treatment of R/R aggressive ATL. Even in clinical practice, valemetostat treatment provides long‐term survival benefits for this dismal disease, with a tolerable safety profile. Therefore, our results highlight that valemetostat is a reliable therapeutic strategy for R/R ATL, especially for responders.

In Japan, Moga monotherapy had changed the treatment strategy of R/R ATL, with a high ORR of 50% in a clinical trial. 30 Nevertheless, Moga was not approved outside of Japan due to its limited efficacy, as evidenced by the European–US clinical trial with an ORR of 11%. 1 , 37 This discrepancy was mainly caused by differences in the inclusion criteria of these trials. The patients enrolled in the latter trial had more aggressive and refractory disease. 37 Indeed, several real‐world Japanese studies that included patients with heavily treated, refractory disease demonstrated that the survival impact of Moga for R/R ATL was limited, 31 , 32 , 34 , 35 , 36 that is, MST is 5.5 months. 34 Therefore, real‐world data are important for more accurately evaluating the efficacy of a novel drug for this dismal disease.

In contrast to the phase II clinical trial of valemetostat, 40 the current study enrolled patients with poor prognoses: (1) The majority of the patients were elderly, with nearly 80% being 70 years or older, and a median age of 74 years (vs. 69 years); (2) 17.9% (vs. 8%) of patients had a poor PS; (3) 17.9% (vs. 0%) of the patients had relapsed after allo‐HSCT, and such relapse is associated with a poor prognosis 28 ; (4) the duration from previous treatment to valemetostat was short, at 35.5 days (vs. 60 days), indicating that the included patients were not able to wait for treatment. Nevertheless, compared to the phase II study, this study found that the median treatment duration and PFS were longer—6.0 months (vs. 4.3 months) and 8.3 months (vs. 7.4 months), respectively—and OS was comparable at a median of 15.8 months (vs. 16.4 months). Although a higher proportion of patients with the unfavourable chronic type were included (21.4% vs. 12.0%), the efficacy of valemetostat was not better for the acute or lymphoma types (Table 2 and Table S2), similar to the results of clinical trial. 40 Thus, our findings confirm the efficacy of valemetostat as a reliable treatment for R/R ATL, even in clinical settings.

Valemetostat may become an especially useful treatment for R/R ATL for three reasons. First, it appears to be more effective than the alternatives. In real‐world settings, the survival durations were longer with valemetostat than with Moga monotherapy (median PFS, 1.8–2.1 months 31 , 32 ; median OS, 4.0–12.0 months 32 , 34 , 35 , 36 ) or tucidinostat (median PFS, 3.95 months; median OS, 8.04 months). 51 Second, Moga use is limited in transplant‐eligible patients with ATL, because pretransplant administration of Moga is associated with increased treatment‐related mortality. 52 Moga has been commonly used as part of the first‐line treatment for transplant‐ineligible patients in Japan, 21 , 22 , 23 but its efficacy in the R/R setting after first‐line Moga‐containing chemotherapy is uncertain. Third, valemetostat demonstrates unique therapeutic properties distinct from those of other agents, 30 , 37 , 39 , 51 showing efficacy in nodal and/or extranodal lesions as well as in refractory disease. Thus, given the favourable efficacy and safety profile of valemetostat demonstrated in this study, valemetostat may be preferred over other agents as a salvage therapy in Japanese clinical practice. Currently, valemetostat is not approved outside of Japan; consequently, the clinical trials are needed in the future.

A notable finding is the comparable survival outcomes for valemetostat in regard to the VCAP‐AMP‐VECP regimen, antiviral therapy and Moga‐CHOP regimen for untreated aggressive ATL (median PFS, 7.0 months, not evaluated and 0.7 years; MST, 12.7 months, 9 months and 1.6 years), 14 , 15 , 16 , 21 although the clinical setting is entirely different. Thus, valemetostat combination therapy may also have the potential to serve as an alternative strategy for first‐line treatment of ATL in the future.

A salient concern in clinical practice pertains to the identification of patients who will benefit from valemetostat. In patients with follicular lymphoma, the progression of disease within 24 months 53 has been identified as a prognostic indicator associated with a poor prognosis. Cutaneous adverse reaction after Moga administration is recognized as a clinical marker that predicts the efficacy of Moga in ATL and CTCL. 21 , 23 , 32 , 36 , 54 , 55 , 56 , 57 Similarly, the present study demonstrates that those identified as responders based on CR and sIL‐2R under ULN following valemetostat administration are likely to have a durable response. The present study did not reveal any other clinical prognostic factors at the time of valemetostat administration, including older age, 51 poor PS, 31 , 34 high LDH, 31 , 34 high sIL‐2R, 51 refractory disease 31 and a history of extensive treatment, 31 as reported for other agents. This may be attributable to the limited sample size in our cohort or to the inherent characteristics of valemetostat. Although this was a retrospective study, according to Schoenfeld's formula, 58 with 13 events (death and/or relapse in this study) and assuming balanced comparisons of two groups, only an HR of ≤0.21 or ≥4.73 could be detected with 80% power at a 5% significance level. Therefore, the present study was likely underpowered to identify more moderate prognostic factors. However, it is noteworthy that valemetostat demonstrated efficacy even in patients who were not expected to respond to other agents, thereby underscoring its potential for diverse patient populations. Further investigations in a larger number of patients and exploration of the molecular mechanisms of valemetostat action 59 are needed to clarify which patients will benefit from valemetostat treatment.

This study had several limitations. First, the number of patients receiving valemetostat treatment was small. Therefore, prognostic factors at the time of valemetostat initiation could not be fully evaluated. However, this study highlights the issues to be addressed in future investigations. Second, the retrospective nature of the study meant that the response of each patient to valemetostat was not evaluated by central review—although the results of the survival analysis support the accurate assessment of treatment response. Third, due to the limited number of transplanted patients and differences in the timing of valemetostat treatment after allo‐HSCT, it is difficult to evaluate the safety of post‐transplant administration of valemetostat. Therefore, further studies with larger cohorts of transplanted patients are needed.

In conclusion, we demonstrate for the first time that valemetostat treatment confers a survival benefit in patients with R/R aggressive ATL, even in clinical practice. This novel finding underscores the idea that valemetostat treatment is a reliable therapeutic strategy, and it changes the treatment paradigm for patients with R/R aggressive ATL, particularly responders. Regrettably, there is still no reliable treatment for the R/R ATL population outside of Japan. Further international studies are warranted to develop novel treatment strategies for this devastating disease.
